title: AI Database Filter
tagline: A local AI assistant that turns plain English into database filters you can check
summary: At my 2026 internship I built a filtering system for a county traffic signal app that covers more than 2,000 signals. You could build filters by hand, or just ask in plain English and a small AI running on our own computer would suggest filters for you to approve. Later I turned it into a shared library so the team could save and share their filters.

hero.alt: Super Filter workspace showing searchable database fields, applied filters, and AI-generated filter proposals side by side
hero.caption: The finished filter workspace: fields, active filters and AI suggestions side by side.

sections.heading: Starting without AI
body: The database had everything about the signals: timing, maintenance, documents, locations, and a lot of tables all connected to each other. Plenty of fields were messy free text too. So before adding any AI, I built the filter builder by hand. It could search text, compare columns, count related records, handle dates, and nest AND, OR and NOT.
Doing that first meant the AI later had a safe, limited set of filters to work with, instead of writing its own SQL.

media.alt: Super Filter open over the traffic-signal application with a map and signal table visible behind it
media.caption: The filter workspace inside the signal app.

sections.heading: Asking in plain English
body: Next I added a chat panel next to the filters. You could ask for something like signals with vehicle detection, and it would come back with filter cards you could approve or deny. It could also read the filters already on screen and fix them.
The AI never touched the database directly. Every suggestion got checked against the real database structure, and queries only ran read-only.

sections.heading: Picking a model that fits
body: The work computer had a 4 GB GPU, which is tiny for AI. The model I started with was accurate but took about 43 seconds to answer. So I built a test harness and ran the same 200 requests across 8 local models, grading every answer. The winner was Qwen2.5 Coder 3B, which fit on the GPU and answered in about 8 seconds.
After about 50 rounds of prompt tweaking, it went from about 85% to 91% on my tests. On a fresh set of messier prompts it improved less, which was a good reminder not to trust a benchmark too much.

media.alt: Windows development workstation showing Ollama running a local model alongside Task Manager and NVIDIA GPU memory usage
media.caption: Ollama running next to the GPU memory meter.

sections.heading: Sharing filters
body: Once people started using it, I didn't want good filters to disappear when you closed the tab. So I added a library where you can save filters and groups of filters, favorite them, and share them with the team by link or in a public catalog. If someone updates a filter you saved, you get a small update notice instead of it changing under you.

sections.heading: Where it ended up
body: It started as a standalone prototype and ended up built into the team's real app. The biggest thing I took from it is that the model was a small part of the work. Most of it was everything around the model: the checks, the testing, and making sure a person always gets the last word.
